# Bayes in Landmark Trials {#sec-landmark}

```{r}
#| include: false
library(ggplot2)
# Posterior probabilities from the SNAP report (Lee et al.): mortality noninferiority, mortality superiority, kidney injury superiority
d <- data.frame(
  claim = factor(c("Mortality: noninferior\n(OR below 1.2)", "Mortality: superior\n(OR below 1.0)",
                   "Kidney injury: superior\n(OR below 1.0)"),
                 levels = rev(c("Mortality: noninferior\n(OR below 1.2)", "Mortality: superior\n(OR below 1.0)",
                                "Kidney injury: superior\n(OR below 1.0)"))),
  p = c(99.2, 89.8, 99.7))
```

Bayesian rules have decided real trials, and in each one the detail mattered: the threshold, the endpoint, and what was fixed before the data arrived.

::: {.callout-important title="Regulatory anchor"}
All documents below are described in @sec-regulatory. Status as of November 2026.

- **FDA draft guidance, Use of Bayesian Methodology in Clinical Trials of Drug and Biological Products (January 2026, draft), Sections III and IV** [@fda_bayesian_2026]. Names REBYOTA, pediatric extrapolation and platform-trial controls among its examples. A draft, so it recommends and does not bind.
- **FDA, Master Protocols for Drug and Biological Product Development, revised draft guidance (June 2026)** [@fda_master_protocols_2026]. Generally no multiplicity adjustment across unrelated drugs in a platform.
- **ICH E11A, Pediatric Extrapolation (Step 4, August 2024)** [@ich_e11a_2024]. Borrowing from adults rests first on the similarity of disease and pharmacology.

The criteria below were agreed for particular development programs. They are not general numerical standards for approval.
:::

| Trial | Disease | Bayesian feature | Decision rule | Outcome |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| I-SPY 2 | Early breast cancer, before surgery | Predictive probability of a later phase 3, up to ten signatures per drug | Graduate at 85%, drop below 10% in all signatures | Neratinib graduated in one signature, pembrolizumab in three |
| REMAP-CAP | Severe pneumonia, COVID-19 | Domains, ordinal model, hierarchical IL-6 effect | Efficacy at a posterior probability above 99% | Tocilizumab met the rule, 99.75% |
| Heparin multiplatform | COVID-19 | Three platforms, one pre-agreed analysis | Superiority above 99%, futility above 95% | Futility in critical illness, superiority otherwise |
| BNT162b2 | COVID-19 prevention | Beta-binomial success rule | VE above 30% with probability above 0.995 (interim) or 0.986 (final) | 8 vs 162 cases, authorized |
| REBYOTA | Recurrent *C. difficile* infection | Discounted borrowing from a phase 2b study | Two thresholds, 0.9750338 and 0.9993275 | 0.991, one threshold met |
| GBM AGILE | Glioblastoma | Seamless phase 2/3 platform | Benefit at least 98%, futility below 25% predictive power | Regorafenib stopped for limited efficacy |
| Pediatric diabetes | Type 2 diabetes in children | Borrowing from adult data | Supportive Bayesian analysis | Empagliflozin indication granted; none for linagliptin |
| DAWN | Stroke, 6 to 24 hours after last known well | Adaptive enrichment, predictive-probability looks | Superiority above 0.986, raised if enriched | Stopped at an interim analysis, 206 patients |
| SNAP | *S. aureus* bacteremia | Hierarchical logistic model, two margins | Noninferiority at OR below 1.2 with posterior probability above 99%, superiority below 1.0 | Noninferiority met, `r sprintf("%.1f", d$p[1])`% |

: The nine trials in this chapter. {#tbl-landmark-summary}

## I-SPY 2: graduation by predictive probability {#sec-landmark-ispy2}

*The question.* Which drugs for early breast cancer deserve a phase 3 trial, and in which kind of tumor? I-SPY 2 has enrolled since 2010 and tests drugs given before surgery against a shared control [@barker2009; @berry2015ispy; @park2016ispy2]. The primary endpoint is pathologic complete response (pCR) at surgery, predicted for patients still in follow-up from tumor volume on MRI.

*The design.* Patients are classified by hormone receptor (HR) status, HER2 status and the MammaPrint gene-expression test. Depending on its biomarker eligibility, a drug is evaluated in up to ten overlapping signatures: all patients, HR+, HR-, HER2+, HER2-, MammaPrint high-2, and the four HER2 by HR combinations. Pembrolizumab was evaluated in three HER2-negative signatures. A covariate-adjusted logistic model for pCR gives the estimates. Randomization is response adaptive within a subtype, with 20% of patients held on control and a planned maximum of 120 patients per experimental arm [@park2016ispy2; @nanda2020effect]. The platform pays for adaptive allocation with a conservative graduation bar and a later confirmatory trial. Methods are in @sec-rar-trials and @sec-platform.

*The decision rule.* A drug *graduates* in a signature when its Bayesian predictive probability of success in a hypothetical 300-patient, equally randomized phase 3 trial reaches 85%. It is dropped for futility only if that probability is below 10% in all of its signatures [@park2016ispy2; @berry2025]. The threshold is not adjusted ten ways. It is set high on purpose, because the authors anticipated that the probability would fall between the interim and the final analysis, once all pathology was in.

*What happened.* Neratinib (127 randomized, of whom 115 were evaluable after 12 withdrew before treatment, against 78 concurrent controls) graduated only in HER2+/HR-, with an estimated pCR of 56% (95% probability interval 37 to 73%) against 33% (11 to 54%) for the trastuzumab control, a probability of superiority of 95%, and a final predictive probability of phase 3 success of 79%, below the 85% bar [@park2016ispy2]. It did not graduate in HER2+/HR+ (30% against 17%, predictive probability 65%) or in all HER2+ patients (39% against 23%, 73%). Pembrolizumab with chemotherapy (69 patients against 181 controls, which accumulated from the platform's opening through closure of that arm and so included nonconcurrent patients, with adjustment for time trends) reached the bar in all three signatures where it was tested, and randomization was halted; the final predictive probabilities were 98.5% (HER2-negative), 99.6% (HR-positive, HER2-negative) and 83.4% (triple negative), and the arm still counts as graduated [@nanda2020effect].

*What regulators accepted.* Nothing about I-SPY 2 is a labeling claim. A graduation is a screening decision that routes a drug to a confirmatory trial, and its false positive rate was calibrated by simulation to be acceptable for a screening stage. FDA's June 2026 master protocol draft does not recommend strong familywise control across different drugs, and I-SPY 2 fits within that position because its per-drug decisions are not familywise claims (@sec-mult-practice).

*Lesson.* A predictive probability ties the decision to the trial that follows. The posterior probability of benefit says whether the effect is positive, and the predictive probability also says whether a trial of a given size would show it. A final predictive probability can fall below the graduation threshold without reversing the earlier decision, and the protocol should say which data enter the calculation and how the final recomputation is treated.

## REMAP-CAP: domains, an ordinal endpoint and the IL-6 result {#sec-landmark-remapcap}

*The question.* How should a critical care network learn about many treatments for severe pneumonia at once, and be ready when a pandemic arrives? REMAP-CAP (Randomized, Embedded, Multifactorial Adaptive Platform trial for Community-Acquired Pneumonia) was designed before COVID-19. An EU-funded network built it after the 2009 H1N1 pandemic, enrollment began in April 2016 (NCT02735707), and a dormant pandemic stratum was activated for COVID-19 [@angus2020remapcap].

*The design.* The platform is organized in *domains*, each a set of alternative interventions for one aspect of care: corticosteroids, antivirals, immune modulators, anticoagulation, antibiotic strategy, ventilation. A patient is randomized in every domain for which he or she is eligible. Each domain has its own appendix and statistical analysis plan, so the master protocol is stable while domains come and go. The trial runs inside routine care and uses routinely collected data where it can. For the pandemic stratum the primary endpoint was organ-support-free days to day 21, an ordinal scale with death as the worst outcome, analyzed with a Bayesian cumulative logistic (proportional-odds) model that has no closed-form posterior. In the interleukin-6 (IL-6) receptor antagonist domain the model adjusted for site, age, sex and time epoch, used neutral priors on the treatment effects, and nested tocilizumab and sarilumab under a shared hierarchical prior on an overall IL-6 antagonist effect, so that each drug borrowed from the other in proportion to how alike their data were [@gordon2021remapcap].

*Randomized evidence from routine care.* REMAP-CAP embeds randomization in routine care, allowing a clinical network to compare accepted treatments while treating eligible patients, so that far more patients inform each answer than a stand-alone trial could enroll [@angus2015fusing]. The case against relying on observational databases instead is in @sec-randomization-failures.

*The decision rule.* Allocation within a domain is updated at prespecified intervals toward arms with a higher posterior probability of being best. The triggers were fixed in advance: superiority if the posterior probability of being best exceeded 99%; efficacy if the probability that the odds ratio against control exceeded 1 was above 99%; futility if the probability that it exceeded 1.2 was below 5%; and equivalence of two non-control arms if the probability of an odds ratio between 0.83 and 1.2 exceeded 90% [@gordon2021remapcap; @angus2020remapcap].

*What happened.* Enrollment in the test of IL-6 receptor antagonists began on 19 April 2020. At the interim analysis of 28 October 2020, tocilizumab met the efficacy criterion: posterior probability of benefit 99.75%, odds ratio 1.87, 95% credible interval 1.20 to 2.76. Assignment to control closed on 19 November, and the final adjusted odds ratio on organ-support-free days was 1.64 (1.25 to 2.14) for tocilizumab [@gordon2021remapcap]. The platform declared that tocilizumab and sarilumab improved outcomes, including survival, in critically ill patients with COVID-19, and kept running (@fig-landmark-timeline).

```{r}
#| label: fig-landmark-timeline
#| fig-cap: "REMAP-CAP in 2020: the IL-6 receptor antagonist domain from its first patient to the closing of the control assignment, and the end of the heparin comparison in critically ill patients."
#| fig-height: 2.8
ev <- data.frame(
  date = as.Date(c("2020-04-19", "2020-10-28", "2020-11-19", "2020-12-19")),
  lab = c("19 Apr\nIL-6 test begins", "28 Oct\nTocilizumab meets\nefficacy rule (99.75%)",
          "19 Nov\nControl assignment\ncloses", "19 Dec\nHeparin stops for futility\n(critically ill)"),
  y = c(1, 1, -1, 1))
ggplot(ev, aes(date, 0)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey50") +
  geom_segment(aes(xend = date, yend = y * 0.6), colour = "grey50") +
  geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  geom_text(aes(y = y * 0.75, label = lab), vjust = ifelse(ev$y > 0, 0, 1), size = 3, lineheight = 0.9) +
  scale_x_date(limits = as.Date(c("2020-03-20", "2021-01-25")), date_breaks = "1 month", date_labels = "%b\n%Y") +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(-1.6, 1.8)) +
  labs(x = "Month (2020 to 2021)", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_blank(), panel.grid = element_blank(), axis.ticks.y = element_blank())
```

*What regulators accepted.* The sources record no regulatory ruling on the IL-6 result. What they do record is the design's position under FDA's June 2026 master protocol draft: the 99% bar was the prespecified criterion for each comparison, and the two drugs share a mechanism, so borrowing between them is defensible, whereas domains testing unrelated treatments are not pooled in the same way (@sec-mult-practice).

*Lesson.* A posterior that is valid at each look lets a platform report a domain while it continues. The model adjusts for calendar time, site and age, which adaptive allocation requires. The main report states a prespecified 99% efficacy criterion. That cutoff alone does not establish the design's frequentist error rates across looks and comparisons. Neutral priors with a 99% efficacy trigger, fixed before the data, were the price of the early report (@sec-priors-remapcap, @sec-bayes-practice).

## The heparin multiplatform trial: three platforms, one analysis {#sec-landmark-heparin}

*The question.* Does therapeutic-dose heparin beat usual-care thromboprophylaxis in COVID-19? Three independently funded Bayesian platforms asked it early in the pandemic: REMAP-CAP, ATTACC (an international platform led from Canada) and ACTIV-4a (United States). Separate reports would have invited conflicting results and a post hoc meta-analysis [@lawler2021anticoag; @goligher2021anticoag].

*The design.* The three teams harmonized their protocols and statistical analysis plans before the data were in, and combined patient-level data in one Bayesian hierarchical model. Two severity cohorts were nested around an overall effect with a neutral mean, with dynamic borrowing across them. The non-critically ill cohort was further divided into high, low and unknown D-dimer groups; stopping criteria were defined for the high and low groups, and none for the unknown group. The outcome was organ-support-free days to day 21 (death scored as -1), analyzed with a cumulative logistic model and weakly informative priors for the baseline probabilities. The shared object was a prespecified analysis, not a shared control group.

*The decision rule.* Randomization continued within each cohort (and, among non-critically ill patients, within the high and low D-dimer groups) until superiority (more than 99% probability that the proportional odds ratio exceeded 1) or futility (more than 95% probability that it was below 1.2). The prespecified sensitivity analysis used an enthusiastic prior centered at an odds ratio of 1.75 (95% credible interval 0.74 to 4.15, prior probability of superiority 90%).

*What happened.* In critically ill patients enrollment stopped on 19 December 2020 at the futility criterion. Of 1207 randomized, primary outcome data were available for 1098; the adjusted odds ratio was 0.83 (95% credible interval 0.67 to 1.03), with a posterior probability of futility of 99.9% [@goligher2021anticoag]. In non-critically ill patients enrollment stopped after an interim analysis of 1398 patients crossed the superiority criteria (above 99%) in both the high and low D-dimer groups. Of 2244 randomized, 2219 were analyzed; the later overall analysis gave a probability of 98.6% that therapeutic dosing increased organ-support-free days (this figure is not the statistic that triggered the stop), with an odds ratio of 1.27 (1.03 to 1.58) [@lawler2021anticoag].

*What regulators accepted.* The sources cited here report no regulatory evaluation of the heparin analysis. The severity strata had been specified in advance, so the opposite findings in the two cohorts were not a post hoc subgroup result.

*Lesson.* The same rule gave opposite stops in two cohorts, and neither is a frequentist boundary. Futility is a narrow claim here: the interval for the critically ill barely includes 1, and the criterion is defined against an odds ratio of 1.2, not against no effect. The posterior is valid at any stopping time, but the chance of a false stop has to be shown by simulation (@sec-simulation, @sec-ch10-practice).

## BNT162b2: a Bayesian success rule behind an authorization {#sec-landmark-bnt}

*The question.* Does the Pfizer and BioNTech mRNA vaccine prevent COVID-19? The phase 2/3 trial (Protocol C4591001) began in July 2020 and reported its efficacy result in the *New England Journal of Medicine* [@polack2020bnt]. The statistical analysis plan on ClinicalTrials.gov makes the primary analysis Bayesian [@pfizer_sap_2020].

*The design.* The model conditions on the total number of first COVID-19 cases, and the cases in the vaccine arm are binomial. The prior, Beta(0.700102, 1), has a mean of 0.4118 (the value at vaccine efficacy of 30%) and an effective sample size of 1.7 cases, so it is centered on the margin and carries almost no weight. The plan calls it minimally informative and says it can be considered pessimistic. Two primary objectives, VE in participants with no evidence of prior infection and VE in all participants, were evaluated in sequence. The final analysis was planned at 164 first confirmed cases, with interim looks. The worked calculation is in @sec-bayes-bnt.

*The decision rule.* Success is $\Pr(\mathrm{VE} > 30\% \mid \text{data})$ above 0.995 at an interim analysis and above 0.986 at the final analysis, with thresholds calibrated so that the overall one-sided type I error is 2.5% [@pfizer_sap_2020]. A nonbinding futility rule allows the trial to stop if the posterior predictive probability of success at the final analysis is 5% or less (for example, at 27.8% observed efficacy with 62 cases and 38.6% with 92 cases). The first interim analysis planned at 32 cases was not performed; the thresholds were unchanged and the SAP states that the type I error remained controlled at 0.025. At the final analysis of 164 cases, 53 vaccine cases is the largest count that still clears 0.986 (@sec-cases-bnt).

*What happened.* There were 8 cases in the vaccine group and 162 in the placebo group, a vaccine efficacy of 95.0% with a 95% credible interval of 90.3 to 97.6% [@polack2020bnt]. The posterior probability that VE exceeded 30% was indistinguishable from one, far above 0.986.

*What regulators accepted.* FDA issued the emergency use authorization on 11 December 2020 for ages 16 and older [@fda_eua_pfizer_2021] and approved the biologics license application (Comirnaty) on 23 August 2021 [@fda2021comirnaty]. FDA's announcements contain no statement on the Bayesian criterion. The binomial model assumes equal surveillance time in the two arms, an approximation that FDA's briefing document adjusts with the surveillance-time ratio.

*Lesson.* The sponsor's posted SAP documents a weak prior with its numbers stated, a margin and thresholds calibrated by simulation. The available version is 10, dated 7 October 2022, so it documents the rules but does not establish when each was first specified. A Bayesian rule on this pattern supported a regulatory action. When the look schedule changed, the sponsor said what stayed fixed (@sec-priors-bnt, @sec-sim-practice, @sec-evalues-practice).

## REBYOTA: one trial standing in for two {#sec-landmark-rebyota}

*The question.* Can one phase 3 trial, with a discounted contribution from an earlier phase 2b study, count as adequate evidence? REBYOTA (RBX2660, fecal microbiota, live-jslm) prevents recurrence of *Clostridioides difficile* infection after antibiotics. The sponsor first planned two phase 3 trials of about 300 patients each. After FDA's July 2013 enforcement discretion on fecal microbiota transplantation made enrollment difficult, it proposed one phase 3 trial (study 2017-01, PUNCH CD3) plus a Bayesian integration of the phase 2b study 2014-01 [@fda_rebyota_briefing_2022].

*The design.* FDA wrote that the studies "are generally exchangeable" but not identical, and accepted a Bayesian hierarchical model with dynamic borrowing, in which the extent of borrowing depends on how similar the effect is in both the active and placebo arms. General hierarchical borrowing models are introduced in @sec-borrowing-hier, and @sec-borrowing-rebyota discusses FDA's data-alignment requests.

*The decision rule.* Success was a posterior probability of superiority with two thresholds, chosen as analogues of one-sided type I error without borrowing. The first, 0.9993275, corresponds to 0.00125, a stricter bar for one trial standing in for two. The second, 0.9750338, corresponds to 0.025, one adequate and well-controlled trial. Both are the values adjusted for the information fraction actually reached.

*What happened.* The modified intention-to-treat success rate was an estimated 0.71 on RBX2660 against 0.57 on placebo (difference 0.13, 95% credible interval 0.02 to 0.24), with a posterior probability of superiority of 0.991. That clears the second threshold and misses the first, so the evidence counts as one adequate and well-controlled trial, not two [@fda_rebyota_briefing_2022].

*What regulators accepted and questioned.* FDA called the approach "acceptable" and approved REBYOTA on 30 November 2022 [@fda_rebyota_2022], on its assessment of the totality of evidence. During the review FDA requested a refined analysis that aligned the success definition, the assessment period (9 weeks in 2014-01 against 8 weeks in 2017-01) and the analysis populations of the old study to those of the new one. The sponsor's primary analysis had also used non-final 2014-01 data, from which six randomized but undosed subjects had been wrongly excluded. Both analyses reached the same conclusion. The briefing gives no borrowing weight or effective sample size, so the amount borrowed cannot be read from it. The January 2026 draft guidance cites REBYOTA as its example of borrowing from an earlier trial of the same drug [@fda_bayesian_2026].

*Lesson.* For this program, FDA agreed two levels of statistical persuasiveness, written in the language of the substantial evidence standard. The observed result met the lower criterion, and approval depended on the totality of evidence. The thresholds were case-specific criteria agreed with FDA, not numerical standards set by statute (@sec-regulatory-practice, @sec-sim-practice). Exchangeability is something the reviewer tests in the data alignment.

## GBM AGILE: a registration platform {#sec-landmark-gbmagile}

*The question.* Can a platform in glioblastoma screen drugs and also produce evidence for registration? GBM AGILE (Adaptive Global Innovative Learning Environment, NCT03970447) was designed with registration in mind, which I-SPY 2 was not [@alexander2018adaptive].

*The design.* A seamless phase 2/3 structure. In stage 1 each arm is randomized adaptively against a shared control (temozolomide in newly diagnosed disease, lomustine in recurrent disease), with arms evaluated monthly. An arm that clears the stage 1 bar graduates to stage 2 with fixed randomization to confirm the finding. Patients are classified into signatures by newly diagnosed versus recurrent disease and MGMT methylation status, [@alexander2018adaptive]. The original platform design reserved 20% of each subtype for control and allowed adaptive allocation among experimental treatments. Regorafenib had an arm-specific exception: allocation remained 1:1 between regorafenib and control throughout enrollment [@wen2026regorafenib]. Registered therapies include regorafenib, paxalisib and VAL-083 [@nct03970447].

*The decision rule.* For regorafenib, the first arm to finish, efficacy required a Bayesian probability of benefit (hazard ratio below 1) of at least 98%. Analyses ran monthly, and the arm stopped enrolling for limited efficacy when the Bayesian predictive power was below 25% in all signatures [@wen2026regorafenib]. The sources cited here document the 98% criterion but not how that cutoff was chosen, so the report does not show its operating characteristics.

*What happened.* Regorafenib stopped for limited efficacy. The median hazard ratios were 1.05, 1.07 and 1.07 (newly diagnosed MGMT-unmethylated, recurrent, and the two combined), with probabilities of benefit of 0.421, 0.312 and 0.296, and the drug had more toxicity than control [@wen2026regorafenib]. The May 2026 erratum added a collaborator to Appendix Table A7 [@wen2026regorafenib_erratum].

*What regulators accepted.* FDA's January 2026 draft cites proposed Bayesian analyses for GBM AGILE and Precision Promise (NCT04229004) that augment concurrent controls with nonconcurrent data while modeling temporal drift [@fda_bayesian_2026; @saville2022]. The draft asks that the simulation report be part of the submission.

*Lesson.* A platform can stop a drug for limited efficacy early and cheaply, and the same machinery that does so is what a registration claim would have to calibrate (@sec-platform, @sec-cases13).

## Pediatric extrapolation: empagliflozin and linagliptin {#sec-landmark-peds}

*The question.* Can the effect of a diabetes drug in adults support its use in children with type 2 diabetes, where a pediatric trial is small? The January 2026 FDA draft guidance names empagliflozin and linagliptin in pediatric type 2 diabetes (the DINAMO program) among its examples of Bayesian methods in use [@fda_bayesian_2026].

*The design and the rule.* DINAMO randomized 158 people aged 10 to 17 with type 2 diabetes, at 108 centers in 15 countries, equally to empagliflozin 10 mg, linagliptin 5 mg or placebo. Participants initially assigned empagliflozin who had not reached HbA1c below 7% at week 12 were rerandomized at week 14 to continue 10 mg or increase to 25 mg, and the primary comparison pooled these dosing groups. The primary outcome was the change in HbA1c (average blood glucose over the previous months) at 26 weeks [@laffel2023dinamo]. Variability in HbA1c turned out larger than planned, which threatened the trial's power, so the sponsor prespecified a supportive Bayesian borrowing analysis [@sailer2025pebb]. Adults could not simply be pooled with children. Instead, models of how each drug is absorbed and how HbA1c responds to drug exposure, fitted to earlier adult and pediatric data, were used to simulate pediatric data, and these formed the informative part of a robust mixture prior (@sec-priors-conflict). External experts and FDA representatives advised on the prior's effective sample size and on the weight of its informative part, and sensitivity analyses covered the full range of weights. Supportive Bayesian superiority required a posterior probability above 97.5% of a placebo-corrected HbA1c reduction, equivalently an upper 97.5% posterior quantile below zero [@sailer2025pebb].

*What happened.* Against placebo, HbA1c fell by 0.84 percentage points with empagliflozin (95% confidence interval 0.19 to 1.50, p = 0.012) and by 0.34 points with linagliptin (95% confidence interval −0.30 to 0.99, p = 0.29) [@laffel2023dinamo]. The borrowing analyses gave posterior means and credible intervals consistent with these results [@sailer2025pebb]. The trial's own analysis therefore carried the empagliflozin result, and the conventional primary analysis for linagliptin was not significant. As reported by Sailer et al., the supportive Bayesian borrowing analysis for linagliptin did meet its prespecified superiority criterion (posterior probability 0.98, posterior mean -0.51 percentage points, upper 95% credible limit -0.05), which depended on an informative prior weight of 0.65 [@sailer2025pebb].

*What regulators accepted.* FDA's January 2026 draft cites these supportive analyses as an example of Bayesian borrowing. It reports that the review team, while noting differences in disease progression between children and adults, judged the pathophysiology of pediatric type 2 diabetes similar to that in adults, so the adult information was relevant to both analyses [@fda_bayesian_2026]. Empagliflozin received a pediatric indication on 20 June 2023, for children aged 10 and older [@fda_peds_t2d_2023]. For linagliptin, FDA considered borrowing from other DPP-4 inhibitor trials more reliable than the sponsor's pharmacometric borrowing analysis; that analysis did not establish efficacy, and linagliptin received no pediatric indication [@fda_linagliptin_peds_review_2023].

*Lesson.* Borrowing from adults is justified by the similarity of disease and pharmacology, and the statistics come second, as ICH E11A says [@ich_e11a_2024]. One way to write the judgment of similarity as a number is a bias between the adult and pediatric effects with a normal distribution of standard deviation $\omega$: a large $\omega$ lets the adult data contribute little, and $\omega = 0$ pools them (@sec-borrowing-pediatric).

## DAWN: an enrichment design that stopped at an early interim look {#sec-landmark-dawn}

*The question.* Does thrombectomy with the Trevo device help patients with a large mismatch between clinical deficit and infarct core when it is done 6 to 24 hours after the patient was last known to be well? [@jovin2017dawn; @nogueira2018thrombectomy]

*The design.* A Bayesian adaptive enrichment design, specified in full in the statistical analysis plan [@stryker_dawn_sap_2017]. The primary endpoint is the 90-day modified Rankin scale (mRS). Two co-primary analyses are nested hierarchically. The first is a utility-weighted mRS, which scores each mRS level by its clinical value and tests superiority on the mean utility (@sec-testing-utility). The second, functional independence (mRS 0 to 2), is tested only if the first succeeds. The design has 86% power for a 1-unit utility effect and a type I error of at most 2.5%.

*The decision rule.* The baseline success threshold is a posterior probability of superiority of 0.986, chosen by simulation to control the type I error, and raised if enrichment occurs, which restricts enrollment to a subgroup irreversibly. The raised threshold is $\Phi\bigl(\sqrt{1 + N_2/(N_1 + N_3)}\;\Phi^{-1}(0.986)\bigr)$, where $N_1$ patients are in the enriched population at the decision, $N_2$ outside it and $N_3$ enrolled after it (@sec-sim-practice). Predictive probability sets the stopping schedule. From 200 randomized patients, with at least 100 since the last enrichment, the trial stops for expected success if the predictive probabilities of success, for both the utility-weighted and the dichotomized mRS, exceed 95% at 200 and 250 patients, 90% at 300 and 350, 85% at 400, and 80% at 450 and 500. For expected-success stopping, the trial predicts whether both primary analyses will succeed after currently enrolled patients complete 90-day follow-up, assuming no further enrollment. It stops for futility if the predictive probability of success after enrollment to the maximum sample size, under any permitted enrichment option, is under 10%. The thresholds fall as the sample grows, so an early stop needs more certainty than a late one (@sec-cases13).

*What happened.* Enrollment stopped 31 months after it began, because of the results of a prespecified interim analysis; the plan's interim analyses began at 150 patients and then came every 50, with stopping for expected success possible from 200, and 206 had been enrolled (107 thrombectomy, 99 control) [@nogueira2018thrombectomy]. The mean utility-weighted mRS was 5.5 against 3.4, an adjusted difference of 2.0 (95% credible interval 1.1 to 3.0), with a posterior probability of superiority above 0.999. Functional independence (mRS 0 to 2) was 49% against 13%, an adjusted difference of 33 points (95% credible interval 24 to 44), with a posterior probability above 0.999 [@nogueira2018thrombectomy].

*What regulators accepted.* The sources cited here include no regulatory review of DAWN. They document the sponsor's side: every threshold, every look, the enrichment rule and its irreversibility, and the predictive-probability bounds were fixed before unblinding, with the type I error a simulation output [@stryker_dawn_sap_2017; @jovin2017dawn].

*Lesson.* A regulator reads the table of looks and thresholds and the simulation that calibrates the final criterion, not the decision theory. A threshold that moves with enrichment has to be calibrated across every enrichment and stopping branch (@sec-predictive, @sec-protocol).

## SNAP: the margin decides the claim {#sec-landmark-snap}

*The question.* Is intravenous cefazolin noninferior to flucloxacillin or cloxacillin, within a margin that allows a small increase in mortality, for adults with penicillin-resistant, methicillin-susceptible *Staphylococcus aureus* (MSSA) bacteremia? The Staphylococcus aureus Network Adaptive Platform (SNAP) trial is an international, pragmatic, open-label Bayesian adaptive platform trial (NCT05137119) at 91 sites in 8 countries [@lee2026snap]. This comparison enrolled adults from 17 February 2022 to 21 June 2024, when recruitment paused because of an acute kidney injury signal. The steering committee accepted closure on 7 August after the noninferiority trigger was met and the safety signal persisted [@lee2026snap].

*The design.* The cefazolin domain randomized 1,341 adults, 671 to cefazolin and 670 to flucloxacillin or cloxacillin, by simple 1:1 randomization (the allocation did not adapt to results). The primary outcome was 90-day all-cause mortality, analyzed with a hierarchical Bayesian logistic regression [@lee2026snap].

*The decision rule.* Scheduled analyses occurred after each additional 500 platform participants reached 90 days. The committee could recommend stopping adult recruitment when the posterior probability that the adjusted mortality odds ratio was below 1.2 exceeded 99% (a margin that, with 15% mortality on the penicillins, is about 2.5 percentage points of absolute mortality). Superiority meant an odds ratio below 1.0, and the futility trigger was a posterior probability of superiority below 1%. The domain stopped after the noninferiority criterion was met (@sec-testing-ni, @sec-borrowing-ni).

*What happened.* Among patients who could be evaluated, mortality at 90 days was 15.0% (97/645) with cefazolin against 17.0% (109/642), an adjusted odds ratio of 0.81 (95% credible interval 0.59 to 1.12). The posterior probability of noninferiority was `r sprintf("%.1f", d$p[1])`% and of superiority `r sprintf("%.1f", d$p[2])`%. Acute kidney injury occurred in 13.9% (92/660) against 19.6% (127/648), an adjusted odds ratio of 0.67 (0.50 to 0.89), with a posterior probability of superiority of 99.7% [@lee2026snap].

```{r}
#| label: fig-landmark-snap
#| fig-cap: "SNAP: posterior probabilities, from the same posterior for mortality, for the two claims tested: no worse than an odds ratio of 1.2, and better."
#| fig-height: 2.6
ggplot(d, aes(p, claim)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.6, fill = "grey35") +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.1f%%", p)), hjust = -0.1, size = 3.5) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 112), breaks = seq(0, 100, 25)) +
  labs(x = "Posterior probability (%)", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank())
```

*What regulators accepted.* The sources cited here include only the published report, and no regulatory assessment of the cefazolin result.

*Lesson.* The same posterior gives `r sprintf("%.1f", d$p[1])`% for "no worse than a 1.2 odds ratio" and `r sprintf("%.1f", d$p[2])`% for "better", so the margin decides the claim. The `r sprintf("%.1f", d$p[2])`% is not a failure of the data. It answers a harder question. A protocol should name the margin, and the probability it requires, before the data are seen.

## Key points {.unnumbered}

- Each trial fixed its decision rule before the data: a posterior or predictive probability, a threshold, and the schedule of looks. Most rules were calibrated by simulation to a stated false-positive rate.
- The quantity differs by purpose. I-SPY 2 used the predictive probability of a later phase 3, at 85%. REMAP-CAP and the heparin trials used posterior probabilities of an odds ratio, at 99%. BNT162b2 used the posterior probability that VE exceeded 30% and DAWN the posterior probability of superiority, both with a final threshold of 0.986 (DAWN's before any enrichment).
- REBYOTA's 0.991 met the one-trial threshold and missed the two-trial threshold, so the evidence counted as one adequate and well-controlled trial, and approval rested on the totality of evidence.
- The heparin trial reached opposite stops in two severity cohorts under one rule, and REMAP-CAP reported the IL-6 result while the platform continued.
- GBM AGILE stopped regorafenib for limited efficacy, with median hazard ratios from 1.05 to 1.07.
- SNAP's posterior gave `r sprintf("%.1f", d$p[1])`% for noninferiority and `r sprintf("%.1f", d$p[2])`% for superiority: the margin decides the claim.
- DAWN stopped at an interim analysis with 206 patients, and its success threshold rises when the population is enriched.

::: {.callout-note title="Discussion questions"}
1. Neratinib's final predictive probability was 79% against an 85% bar, yet it graduated in one signature. Explain why the rule can be satisfied at an interim and missed at the final analysis, and what a protocol should say about it.
2. REBYOTA's posterior probability of 0.991 met one threshold and missed another. Which claim does each threshold support, and why should the thresholds be written before the data?
3. SNAP gave `r sprintf("%.1f", d$p[1])`% for noninferiority and `r sprintf("%.1f", d$p[2])`% for superiority from one posterior. Suppose the noninferiority margin had been an odds ratio of 1.1. What would you expect to happen to the first number, and what would you want the protocol to say?
4. REMAP-CAP and the heparin trials used a 99% efficacy trigger and a 95% futility trigger against an odds ratio of 1.2. Why are these two numbers not the same, and what does futility claim in the critically ill cohort?
5. DAWN raises its success threshold when it enriches the population. What would go wrong if the threshold stayed at 0.986?
:::
